screens.title: BGP Fundamentals: AS Numbers, Peers, and Message Types
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we’ll make the mechanics of BGP concrete. You will learn how Autonomous System numbers and neighbor types shape whether BGP sessions are internal or external, how the TCP transport and port 179 bring the session to life, and the five message types that carry negotiation, routing updates, keepalives, error notices, and refresh requests. Understanding these pieces is essential because BGP is the protocol that moves routing policy and reachability across organizational boundaries; small configuration mistakes cause sessions to stall or routes to disappear. For example, an eBGP session with your ISP expects a one‑hop neighbor and will fail if the remote AS is typed incorrectly. Likewise, iBGP sessions often use loopback addresses and depend on the underlying IGP for reachability. We’ll also walk through the neighbor state machine you’ll observe in the router CLI and common troubleshooting checks such as verifying TCP port 179 and AS numbers. By the end you’ll be able to explain why iBGP has a split‑horizon rule, when to use ebgp‑multihop, and how to interpret OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, and ROUTE‑REFRESH messages. Keep an eye out for the practical examples; they mirror typical lab scenarios you’ll replicate in a simulator.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › BGP Fundamentals
BGP Fundamentals: AS Numbers, Peers, and Message Types
Understand how BGP peers form sessions, the five message types they exchange, and the neighbor states you will see when troubleshooting.
Why this matters
Correct peering avoids outages and policy leaks. Misconfigured AS or blocked port 179 prevents session establishment and route exchange.
In this lesson
  • Distinguish eBGP and iBGP use cases and defaults.
  • Explain BGP's TCP transport and port 179 behavior.
  • Identify OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, ROUTE‑REFRESH roles.
  • Interpret neighbor states and common troubleshooting checks.
Coming up
Hands-on: simulate a misconfigured neighbor and watch the state machine move from Active back to Connect, then fix the ASN to reach Established.
Visual concept
Peer Types
eBGP: different AS • iBGP: same AS
Messages
OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, ROUTE-REFRESH
Neighbor States
Idle → Connect → Active → OpenSent → OpenConfirm → Established
Explore Key Topics
eBGP vs iBGP
When peers are in different ASs, you use eBGP; within the same AS use iBGP and plan for full mesh or route reflectors.
BGP Messages
OPEN negotiates session parameters; UPDATE carries routes and attributes; KEEPALIVE maintains liveness.
Neighbor States
Read states with show ip bgp summary to identify where handshakes fail.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: Over the next screens we’ll make four measurable learning outcomes clear. First, you will distinguish eBGP from iBGP: know when to peer across different Autonomous Systems and when to peer within the same AS. This matters because it changes defaults such as expected one‑hop neighbors and the need for loopback peering. Second, you will explain the process by which BGP neighbors establish a session using TCP. You’ll understand that a TCP handshake on port 179 is the foundation, and that BGP messages follow only after TCP succeeds. Both skills are useful when reading router output to determine whether the problem is at TCP level or at BGP negotiation. Each objective also includes a practical mnemonic and a verified competency checkpoint so you can self‑assess. Expect hands‑on checks like using telnet to port 179 and reading the neighbor state in the BGP summary. A common misconception I’ll correct: eBGP being one hop by default does not mean you cannot peer across multiple hops — ebgp‑multihop exists but has specific implications. Keep these objectives in mind as we step through the messages and states.

screens.title: eBGP vs iBGP — What changes when peers cross AS boundaries
screens.narratorSegment: Start with a clear claim: eBGP peerings are between routers in different Autonomous Systems and iBGP peerings are between routers in the same Autonomous System. That distinction matters because it changes default behavior and operational practice. eBGP typically expects neighbors to be directly connected and therefore uses a one‑hop TTL expectation; when you must peer across multiple hops, you use ebgp‑multihop to allow the session to form. In practice you use eBGP to exchange routes with an ISP or another organization. iBGP, in contrast, is used to propagate external routes throughout a single AS so internal routers have consistent views of routes learned from the outside. Because of the iBGP split‑horizon rule — a router will not advertise a route learned from an iBGP peer to another iBGP peer — iBGP requires additional design: either a full mesh of peerings or mechanisms like Route Reflectors and Confederations, which we will study later. Concrete example: you peer with ISP ASN 65002 using eBGP on a physical interface; inside your AS 65001, your internal routers use iBGP loopback peering so the session survives an interface flap. A common misconception is to assume iBGP will automatically re‑advertise internal updates the same way an IGP would; it will not, and that leads to inconsistent route propagation if you do not plan the mesh. Takeaway: know the peer type first — it changes everything about address choice, TTL expectations, and design constraints.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › eBGP vs iBGP
eBGP
External peers — different AS
  • Default one‑hop neighbor expectation; often directly connected.
  • Used to exchange routes between organizations or ISPs.
  • ebgp‑multihop required only when peers are not directly connected.
Concrete example
Peer with ISP ASN 65002 on a physical interface; remote‑as configured to 65002.
iBGP
Internal peers — same AS
  • Used to distribute external learnings inside an AS.
  • Does not re‑advertise routes learned from iBGP to other iBGP peers (split‑horizon).
  • Often uses loopback addresses and requires IGP reachability.
Concrete example
Routers in ASN 65001 peer via loopback to keep sessions stable when interfaces flap.
Key takeaway
Choose peer type first; your topology, TTL, and session source address flow from that decision.
Common mistake
Assuming iBGP will re‑advertise to other iBGP peers like an IGP does — it won’t without full mesh or reflectors.
Pro tip
When using loopbacks for iBGP, ensure the IGP advertises them and configure update‑source to match.

screens.title: eBGP operational details and ebgp-multihop
screens.narratorSegment: Let's look closer at eBGP behavior and the ebgp‑multihop exception. By design, an eBGP session usually assumes the peers are directly connected. That simplifies trust and topology: the router expects the neighbor’s IP to be reachable on the directly attached network, and the Time‑To‑Live or TTL checks in many implementations reflect a one‑hop assumption. When you cannot establish a direct physical adjacency — for example, when an ISP hands you an address reachable across one or more transit devices — you may configure ebgp‑multihop to allow the TCP connection across multiple hops. Use ebgp‑multihop cautiously: it changes the failure semantics and can allow unintended neighbors to establish sessions if routing or ACLs are misconfigured. A concrete scenario: two routers in different ASs are separated by a transit switch; without ebgp‑multihop the TCP connection would not form because the default TTL would expire or the neighbor check would fail. Add ebgp‑multihop to permit the session, but also restrict the peer IP via ACLs and verify the remote AS with neighbor remote‑as. A common misconception is to use ebgp‑multihop as a convenience without tightening access controls — that can create security and stability risks. Takeaway: ebgp‑multihop is a tool for special topologies, not a default.

keyIdea.title: eBGP one-hop
keyIdea.text: eBGP presumes direct neighbors; use ebgp‑multihop only when necessary and with access controls to avoid unintended sessions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › eBGP operational details
Process: eBGP session expectation
  1. Configure neighbor with remote‑as of the external peer.
  2. TCP attempts to connect to port 179; default behavior expects direct reachability.
  3. On success, BGP messages begin; on failure consider TTL or ACL blocks.
When to use ebgp‑multihop
Non‑direct physical paths, managed transit, or when peering across WAN links where direct adjacency is impossible.
Checklist & example
Checklist: confirm remote‑as, ensure ACLs permit TCP 179, use ebgp‑multihop only if required, and lock the peer IP with inbound filters.
Example scenario
Two ASs separated by transit devices: configure neighbor x.x.x.x remote‑as 65002 and set ebgp‑multihop if the path is multi‑hop, then restrict reachability with ACLs to the peer IP.
Common mistake
Enabling ebgp‑multihop without limiting the peer address can allow unexpected neighbors to connect.
Tip
Add an access list permitting only the remote peer IP to port 179 when using ebgp‑multihop.
Key takeaway
Use ebgp‑multihop only for topologies that require it and secure the peer with filters.

screens.title: iBGP design: loopback peering, update-source, and split-horizon
screens.narratorSegment: iBGP requires deliberate design choices because routers within the same Autonomous System must share routes learned externally without creating loops. Start with loopback peering: operators often configure iBGP sessions using loopback addresses as neighbor endpoints so the BGP session remains stable despite physical interface failures. However, using loopbacks changes the source IP of the TCP connection, so you must configure update‑source Loopback0 on the neighbor statement to force the router to use the loopback as the source. Equally important is reachability: the underlying IGP, such as OSPF or EIGRP, must correctly advertise those loopback addresses so the TCP connection can be established. The iBGP split‑horizon rule says a router will not advertise a route learned from one iBGP peer to another iBGP peer. That prevents loops but makes a naive iBGP deployment require a full mesh of peerings — every iBGP router peers with every other router — which scales as N*(N-1)/2. For larger networks, Route Reflectors or Confederations are used to reduce mesh requirements; we will cover those in a later chapter. A common troubleshooting mistake is forgetting to add update‑source, which leaves the neighbor stuck in Active because the source IP used by TCP does not match the configured neighbor IP. Takeaway: for stable iBGP, ensure loopback reachability, update‑source configuration, and an architectural plan for distribution.

keyIdea.title: iBGP essentials
keyIdea.text: Loopback peering with update‑source and IGP reachability plus a plan to avoid N^2 peerings are core to iBGP design.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › iBGP Design
Architecture: iBGP with loopbacks
Workflow: configure neighbor using loopback IP, configure neighbor update‑source Loopback0, and ensure IGP advertises the loopbacks so TCP can reach the remote source.
Why update‑source matters
Without update‑source, the router will source the TCP connection from a physical interface address that does not match the expected loopback neighbor IP, preventing the TCP handshake.
Split‑horizon rule
A router will not advertise a route learned via iBGP to another iBGP peer. This prevents loops but requires distribution design.
Scaling
Full mesh grows as N*(N-1)/2. Use Route Reflectors or Confederations to avoid full mesh — topics in later chapters.
Example configuration
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 remote-as 65001
 neighbor 10.0.0.2 update-source Loopback0
Ensure IGP advertises the loopbacks so 10.0.0.2 is reachable before peering.
Common mistake
Omitting update‑source when peering to loopbacks leaves the neighbor stuck in Active.
Pro tip
Always verify loopback routes in the IGP before troubleshooting BGP.
Key takeaway
iBGP requires source control and IGP reachability; plan distribution to avoid full mesh complexity.

screens.title: BGP transport: TCP and port 179
screens.narratorSegment: BGP is built on top of TCP and uses port 179 as its standard transport. That means BGP relies on TCP’s reliable byte stream for ordered delivery and connection management; BGP messages are exchanged only after the TCP three‑way handshake completes. Practically, this implies that most session problems are TCP problems: if you cannot connect to port 179, the routers will not exchange OPEN messages and the neighbor state often remains in Connect or Active. A concrete troubleshooting step is to test TCP reachability with a telnet to port 179 from the router or an intermediary host. If telnet to 179 fails, inspect ACLs, firewall rules, or routing that prevents the source IP from reaching the peer. On iBGP with loopbacks, verify that the source address used for TCP is reachable and that update‑source was configured. Another common issue is incorrect remote‑as settings: if the remote AS does not match what the neighbor expects, the session may form TCP but fail during OPEN negotiation. Therefore, start by confirming TCP connectivity, then move to BGP message exchange and configuration. Misconception to avoid: assuming that BGP will retry infinitely without examining the underlying TCP connection or access controls — often the root cause is network reachability, not BGP syntax. Takeaway: when in doubt, validate TCP first, then BGP.

keyIdea.text: Always verify TCP connectivity to port 179 before deep BGP debugging; many BGP failures are caused by TCP or ACL issues.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › BGP Transport
Why TCP matters
Because BGP rides on TCP, ordered delivery and connection state come from TCP, not BGP. BGP opens its session only after a successful TCP handshake on port 179.
Quick troubleshooting steps
  • Attempt telnet 179 to test TCP reachability.
  • Inspect ACLs and firewall rules blocking port 179.
  • On iBGP, confirm update‑source and IGP reachability to loopback IPs.
Example check
! From router CLI
telnet 192.0.2.2 179
If the connection fails, the router cannot start BGP negotiation. Fix TCP or routing before debugging BGP messages.
Note
Remote‑as mismatch can allow TCP then fail at OPEN; check both TCP and AS values.
Pro tip
Check the source IP used for the TCP connection when using loopbacks — it must be reachable to the peer.
Key takeaway
TCP reachability is necessary and often sufficient to decide whether the problem is network-level or BGP-level.

screens.title: The five BGP message types and their roles
screens.narratorSegment: BGP defines five message types that drive session negotiation and route exchange. First is the OPEN message. Sent after the TCP handshake, OPEN negotiates version, the sender’s ASN, hold time, and router ID. If the parameters are invalid, the session will not establish. Second is UPDATE, the workhorse message that advertises and withdraws routes. An UPDATE contains prefixes plus a set of path attributes that describe characteristics and history for each route; path attributes allow policy decisions beyond simple reachability. Third is KEEPALIVE, a small periodic message sent to prevent Hold Time expiration and confirm the peer is alive. Fourth is NOTIFICATION: when a fatal error or protocol violation occurs, a NOTIFICATION is sent and the session terminates. Finally, ROUTE‑REFRESH requests a peer to re‑advertise routes, useful after applying a new policy without tearing down the session. Concrete example: after establishing TCP and exchanging OPEN messages, peers will exchange UPDATEs carrying prefixes; if you change policy and need new advertisements, you can request a ROUTE‑REFRESH rather than reset the whole session. Misconception: KEEPALIVE is not optional — without it the Hold Time will expire and the session will be declared down. Takeaway: each message has a distinct operational role and you will see them in debug output during session establishment and maintenance.

keyIdea.title: Message roles
keyIdea.text: OPEN negotiates; UPDATE advertises routes; KEEPALIVE proves liveness; NOTIFICATION signals fatal errors; ROUTE‑REFRESH requests re‑advertisement after policy changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › BGP Message Types
OPEN
First message after TCP; negotiates BGP version, remote ASN, Hold Time, and Router ID. If mismatch occurs, session fails.
UPDATE
Carries route advertisements and withdrawals, plus BGP path attributes used for policy decisions.
KEEPALIVE
Periodic liveness message sent to avoid Hold Time expiry; keeps the session alive between UPDATEs.
NOTIFICATION
Sent when a fatal error is detected; causes session termination and often includes an error code.
ROUTE‑REFRESH
Requests a peer to resend its route advertisements, which is useful after applying new policy so you do not need to flap the session.
Example
After OPEN succeeds, UPDATE messages share prefixes. If you change filters, request ROUTE‑REFRESH to reapply policy without resetting the session.
Misconception
KEEPALIVE is not merely optional; without it the Hold Time will expire and the neighbor will be considered down.
Key takeaway
Recognize each message by function: negotiation, advertisement, liveness, error, and refresh.

screens.title: OPEN and UPDATE messages — what they negotiate and carry
screens.narratorSegment: Now focus on the two messages you will most frequently reason about during session setup and routing: OPEN and UPDATE. OPEN is the negotiation handshake that follows TCP. It includes the sender’s ASN, the BGP version, Hold Time, and Router ID. If the Hold Time values differ, routers will agree on a value or refuse the connection depending on implementation; mismatched AS values cause the OPEN to be rejected. Once OPEN succeeds, UPDATE messages exchange routing information. An UPDATE advertises new reachable prefixes and can also withdraw previously announced routes. Critically, each UPDATE carries a set of BGP path attributes — pieces of metadata such as AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, and others — that describe the route’s history and guide policy decisions. We will cover full attribute semantics in the next chapter, but for now remember that UPDATEs are far richer than a simple prefix list. Concrete example: when two peers come up, you might see an OPEN exchange then a stream of UPDATEs advertising the ISP's prefixes; when you apply a filter that removes certain routes, UPDATEs will send withdrawals for those prefixes. Misconception: UPDATEs do not only add routes; they also withdraw; watching both adds and withdraws is vital in debugging. Takeaway: OPEN sets the rules, UPDATE exchanges the data and policy-relevant attributes.

keyIdea.title: OPEN vs UPDATE
keyIdea.text: OPEN negotiates parameters and accepts the peer; UPDATE carries the routing data and attributes needed for policy decisions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › OPEN & UPDATE
OPEN message — negotiation
Contains ASN, BGP version, Hold Time, and Router ID. If the ASN is wrong or parameters conflict, the session will fail during OPEN handling.
Checklist
  • Confirm neighbor remote‑as matches peer ASN.
  • Verify Router ID and Hold Time expectations where relevant.
UPDATE message — routing and attributes
Carries prefixes to advertise and withdrawals. Includes path attributes used by policy to select and manipulate routes.
Note
Path attributes are the reason BGP supports policy-based routing across AS boundaries; they contain history and preference signals.
Example flow
TCP handshake → OPEN exchange → KEEPALIVE → UPDATE messages with prefixes from the ISP. If policy changes, subsequent UPDATEs withdraw and re-advertise as needed.
Misconception
Assuming UPDATEs only add routes. UPDATEs also withdraw; both must be monitored when debugging route changes.

screens.title: KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, and ROUTE‑REFRESH behavior
screens.narratorSegment: KEEPALIVE messages are the heartbeat of a BGP session. Sent periodically, they prevent the Hold Time timer from expiring. Without timely KEEPALIVEs or UPDATEs the peer will consider the neighbor down when the Hold Timer lapses. NOTIFICATION messages are sent when a router detects a fatal error; upon sending or receiving a NOTIFICATION the session is terminated so you can inspect the error code and reason. Practical debugging often encounters NOTIFICATIONs when an OPEN parameter mismatches or a malformed UPDATE is received. ROUTE‑REFRESH is a useful operational message: when you change route policies you can request a peer to re‑advertise its routes instead of tearing down the session. That helps avoid route flaps and preserves session state while policies take effect. A concrete operational example: after changing inbound filters you might use ROUTE‑REFRESH to ask the neighbor to resend its routes so your new filters are applied. A frequent misconception is that ROUTE‑REFRESH is mandatory on older implementations; modern BGP implementations support it as a standard mechanism to avoid session resets. Takeaway: KEEPALIVE maintains liveness, NOTIFICATION ends sessions with an error, and ROUTE‑REFRESH helps you reapply policy without resetting BGP.

keyIdea.title: Maintenance messages
keyIdea.text: KEEPALIVE keeps sessions alive; NOTIFICATION reports fatal errors; ROUTE‑REFRESH triggers re‑advertisement after policy changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › KEEPALIVE / NOTIFICATION / REFRESH
KEEPALIVE
Periodic message to prevent Hold Time expiration. Sent even when no UPDATEs are present to indicate peer is alive.
NOTIFICATION
Sent to indicate a fatal protocol error; receiving a NOTIFICATION ends the session and provides an error code for diagnostics.
ROUTE‑REFRESH
Requests peers to re-advertise routes so new policies can be applied without resetting the session.
Example
Apply a new inbound filter and request ROUTE‑REFRESH to have the neighbor resend its routes under the new policy.
Common mistake
Ignoring NOTIFICATION codes; they point to why the session closed and speed troubleshooting.
Key takeaway
Use ROUTE‑REFRESH to apply policy changes without session downtime; read NOTIFICATIONs to identify fatal protocol issues.

screens.title: Neighbor state machine: Idle → Established
screens.narratorSegment: The BGP neighbor state machine is the best place to start when sessions fail. It progresses through well‑defined states: Idle is the initial state where the process is not attempting a connection or is waiting to retry after an error. Connect means the process is waiting for the TCP connection to complete. Active indicates the process is actively trying to make a TCP connection; if TCP succeeds it moves to OpenSent. OpenSent means an OPEN was sent and the router awaits the peer's OPEN. OpenConfirm follows once an OPEN from the peer is received and the router waits for a KEEPALIVE or NOTIFICATION. Established is the final operational state where UPDATEs may be exchanged. Concrete troubleshooting workflow: if the neighbor is in Active or Connect, validate TCP to port 179, firewall rules, and routing to the neighbor. If it hangs in OpenSent or OpenConfirm, examine the OPEN parameters such as remote‑as and Router ID or use debug to watch OPEN and KEEPALIVE exchanges. A common misconception is to jump into BGP policy debugging while the neighbor never reached Established; policy is irrelevant until the session is up. Takeaway: map the observed state to the correct troubleshooting layer — TCP and reachability for Active/connect, OPEN validation for OpenSent/OpenConfirm, and UPDATE/policy for Established.

keyIdea.title: State mapping
keyIdea.text: Use neighbor state to focus troubleshooting: TCP issues in Active/Connect, OPEN negotiation issues in OpenSent/OpenConfirm, and routing policy after Established.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Neighbor States
Timeline: neighbor state progression
Idle
Initial state or waiting for retry after an error.
Connect
Waiting for TCP to complete; check TCP reachability.
Active
Actively trying TCP; often a sign TCP is failing repeatedly.
OpenSent
OPEN sent; waiting for peer OPEN. Check ASN and OPEN parameters if stuck.
OpenConfirm
OPEN received and acknowledged; waiting for KEEPALIVE or NOTIFICATION.
Established
Session is up; UPDATEs can be exchanged.
Troubleshooting quick map
  • Active/Connect → Verify TCP port 179, firewall, ACLs, routing.
  • OpenSent/OpenConfirm → Check remote‑as and OPEN parameters, use debug if safe.
  • Established → Inspect UPDATEs, path attributes, and apply policies carefully.
Common pitfall
Trying to debug policy while the neighbor is still in Active — fix reachability first.
Pro tip
Use show ip bgp summary and show ip bgp neighbors to map state and next checks quickly.
Key takeaway
Map observed neighbor state to the correct troubleshooting layer to save time.

screens.title: Hands-on: Simulate misconfiguration and observe BGP states
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the hands‑on scenario provided in the chapter. You will configure two routers connected over a LAN and intentionally misconfigure the remote ASN on one side. On R1 you set router bgp 65001 and neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote‑as 65003. Because R2 is not configured or has a different ASN, the BGP neighbor will not reach Established; you’ll observe the neighbor in Active or OpenSent depending on whether TCP succeeds. The practical steps are: configure IP addresses on the connected interfaces, apply the first BGP configuration on R1 with the wrong remote‑as, and run show ip bgp summary to observe the neighbor state. Then configure R2 with router bgp 65002 and neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote‑as 65001; note the states shift but still may not reach Established until ASNs match. Finally correct R1’s neighbor configuration to remote‑as 65002 and watch the session transition to Established. Use debug ip bgp to observe OPEN, KEEPALIVE, and UPDATE messages during transitions. A common mistake is to forget to undo the incorrect neighbor before reconfiguring, which can leave stale entries; using no neighbor to remove entries is safe practice. Takeaway: the exercise reinforces the sequence: fix TCP and ASNs first, then inspect messages with debug.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Lab Walkthrough
Scenario steps
  1. Configure interfaces: R1: 192.168.12.1/24, R2: 192.168.12.2/24.
  2. On R1 configure BGP with wrong remote‑as to simulate failure.
  3. Run show ip bgp summary to observe Active or Connect.
  4. Configure R2 with remote‑as 65002 and then correct R1 to match; observe Established.
  5. Use debug ip bgp to watch OPEN, KEEPALIVE, and UPDATE during change.
Example config snippets
! On R1 (intentional wrong AS)
router bgp 65001
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65003

! On R2 (correct AS for later)
router bgp 65002
 neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote-as 65001

! Fix on R1 to match R2
router bgp 65001
 no neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65003
 neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote-as 65002
Safety note
Use debug sparingly on production devices. In the lab it helps reveal OPEN and KEEPALIVE exchanges during state transitions.
Checklist
Verify IP addressing, TCP 179, remote‑as values, and then use debug to inspect messages.
Key takeaway
Reproduce a misconfiguration to see the state machine in action; correcting ASN and TCP reachability usually restores the session.

screens.title: Common mistakes and a practical troubleshooting checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When a BGP session fails, a systematic checklist saves time. Start with TCP: confirm connectivity to port 179 from the router or an intermediary host using telnet and show tcp brief. If TCP fails, inspect ACLs and firewalls before touching BGP. Next confirm ASNs: an incorrect neighbor remote‑as will block OPEN negotiation; ensure the remote‑as matches the intended peer. For iBGP, verify update‑source configuration and that the underlying IGP advertises the loopback addresses. A frequent real‑world error is forgetting to configure update‑source when peering to loopbacks — TCP may be sourced from a different IP than the configured neighbor, keeping the session in Active. Also verify that the correct interface addresses are used in neighbor statements and consider ebgp‑multihop only when necessary. Use show ip bgp neighbors to read the last error or NOTIFICATION code if the session dies. As a concrete checklist: 1) telnet to port 179, 2) verify route to neighbor IP, 3) check remote‑as values, 4) confirm update‑source for loopback peers, 5) review ACLs and firewall rules. Misconception: jumping to BGP policy changes before ensuring TCP and ASN correctness wastes time. Takeaway: work from transport up to BGP messages, and use the neighbor state to guide the checks.

keyIdea.text: Validate TCP to port 179, confirm ASNs, ensure loopback reachability and update‑source, then inspect BGP messages and NOTIFICATION codes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.2 › Troubleshooting
Step-by-step checklist
  1. Test TCP: telnet 179 or show tcp brief.
  2. Confirm IP reachability to neighbor (ping or traceroute).
  3. Verify neighbor remote‑as value matches expected ASN.
  4. For iBGP, ensure update‑source and IGP reachability of loopbacks.
  5. Check ACLs and firewall rules that might block port 179.
  6. Use show ip bgp neighbors and debug ip bgp to inspect OPEN, KEEPALIVE, UPDATE, or NOTIFICATION activity.
Common errors
  • Wrong remote‑as configured on one side.
  • Missing update‑source for loopback peers.
  • Firewalls or ACLs blocking TCP 179.
  • Assuming iBGP will re-advertise iBGP-learned routes without reflectors.
Practical tip
Start with TCP checks. If TCP succeeds, then open BGP diagnostics. This order saves time.
Pitfall
Changing policies while sessions are not Established confuses diagnostics — get sessions up first.
Key takeaway
A methodical transport->session->policy approach yields faster, more reliable troubleshooting.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Keep six core ideas top of mind as you work with BGP. First, eBGP is for peers in different Autonomous Systems and normally expects one‑hop adjacency. Second, iBGP is for peers within the same AS and requires planning because routers will not re‑advertise iBGP‑learned routes to other iBGP peers. Third, BGP uses TCP on port 179; when a session fails, verify TCP connectivity before deep BGP debugging. Fourth, the OPEN message negotiates session parameters and must match in meaningful ways for the session to form. Fifth, UPDATE messages carry prefixes and path attributes used for policy decisions, not just simple reachability. Sixth, KEEPALIVE preserves liveness and NOTIFICATION reports fatal errors. These concepts are foundational: use them as mental checks during configuration and troubleshooting. Ask yourself after each failure whether the problem is transport, negotiation, or routing policy, and that will guide your next steps.

Peers in different ASs; usually one hop and direct adjacency.

When a BGP problem appears, work from transport (TCP) to negotiation (OPEN) to routing data (UPDATE) so you can isolate the root cause quickly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll make the mechanics of BGP concrete. You will learn how Autonomous System numbers and neighbor types shape whether BGP sessions are internal or external, how the TCP transport and port 179 bring the session to life, and the five message types that carry negotiation, routing updates, keepalives, error notices, and refresh requests. Understanding these pieces is essential because BGP is the protocol that moves routing policy and reachability across organizational boundaries; small configuration mistakes cause sessions to stall or routes to disappear. For example, an eBGP session with your ISP expects a one‑hop neighbor and will fail if the remote AS is typed incorrectly. Likewise, iBGP sessions often use loopback addresses and depend on the underlying IGP for reachability. We’ll also walk through the neighbor state machine you’ll observe in the router CLI and common troubleshooting checks such as verifying TCP port 179 and AS numbers. By the end you’ll be able to explain why iBGP has a split‑horizon rule, when to use ebgp‑multihop, and how to interpret OPEN, UPDATE, KEEPALIVE, NOTIFICATION, and ROUTE‑REFRESH messages. Keep an eye out for the practical examples; they mirror typical lab scenarios you’ll replicate in a simulator.

Over the next screens we’ll make four measurable learning outcomes clear. First, you will distinguish eBGP from iBGP: know when to peer across different Autonomous Systems and when to peer within the same AS. This matters because it changes defaults such as expected one‑hop neighbors and the need for loopback peering. Second, you will explain the process by which BGP neighbors establish a session using TCP. You’ll understand that a TCP handshake on port 179 is the foundation, and that BGP messages follow only after TCP succeeds. Both skills are useful when reading router output to determine whether the problem is at TCP level or at BGP negotiation. Each objective also includes a practical mnemonic and a verified competency checkpoint so you can self‑assess. Expect hands‑on checks like using telnet to port 179 and reading the neighbor state in the BGP summary. A common misconception I’ll correct: eBGP being one hop by default does not mean you cannot peer across multiple hops — ebgp‑multihop exists but has specific implications. Keep these objectives in mind as we step through the messages and states.

This second objectives sheet turns the four outcomes into practice checks and clarifies common pitfalls. For differentiating eBGP and iBGP, you should be able to explain why eBGP peers are normally one hop away and why iBGP peers often use loopbacks and rely on the IGP for reachability. For TCP session setup, you will routinely verify connectivity to port 179 and recognize when the problem is TCP-level rather than BGP-level. For the message types, you will identify which message starts the session (OPEN), which moves routing information (UPDATE), which preserves liveness (KEEPALIVE), which reports fatal errors (NOTIFICATION), and which requests a policy-triggered re-advertisement (ROUTE‑REFRESH). For neighbor states, you will practice reading show ip bgp summary and map observed states to actions — for example, Active often means TCP cannot complete. Each card includes a verification milestone: perform a telnet to 179, check neighbor AS numbers, and confirm loopback reachability. Practice these checks in the simulator to build the habit of isolating TCP problems first and then examining BGP messages and configuration.

Start with a clear claim: eBGP peerings are between routers in different Autonomous Systems and iBGP peerings are between routers in the same Autonomous System. That distinction matters because it changes default behavior and operational practice. eBGP typically expects neighbors to be directly connected and therefore uses a one‑hop TTL expectation; when you must peer across multiple hops, you use ebgp‑multihop to allow the session to form. In practice you use eBGP to exchange routes with an ISP or another organization. iBGP, in contrast, is used to propagate external routes throughout a single AS so internal routers have consistent views of routes learned from the outside. Because of the iBGP split‑horizon rule — a router will not advertise a route learned from an iBGP peer to another iBGP peer — iBGP requires additional design: either a full mesh of peerings or mechanisms like Route Reflectors and Confederations, which we will study later. Concrete example: you peer with ISP ASN 65002 using eBGP on a physical interface; inside your AS 65001, your internal routers use iBGP loopback peering so the session survives an interface flap. A common misconception is to assume iBGP will automatically re‑advertise internal updates the same way an IGP would; it will not, and that leads to inconsistent route propagation if you do not plan the mesh. Takeaway: know the peer type first — it changes everything about address choice, TTL expectations, and design constraints.

Let's look closer at eBGP behavior and the ebgp‑multihop exception. By design, an eBGP session usually assumes the peers are directly connected. That simplifies trust and topology: the router expects the neighbor’s IP to be reachable on the directly attached network, and the Time‑To‑Live or TTL checks in many implementations reflect a one‑hop assumption. When you cannot establish a direct physical adjacency — for example, when an ISP hands you an address reachable across one or more transit devices — you may configure ebgp‑multihop to allow the TCP connection across multiple hops. Use ebgp‑multihop cautiously: it changes the failure semantics and can allow unintended neighbors to establish sessions if routing or ACLs are misconfigured. A concrete scenario: two routers in different ASs are separated by a transit switch; without ebgp‑multihop the TCP connection would not form because the default TTL would expire or the neighbor check would fail. Add ebgp‑multihop to permit the session, but also restrict the peer IP via ACLs and verify the remote AS with neighbor remote‑as. A common misconception is to use ebgp‑multihop as a convenience without tightening access controls — that can create security and stability risks. Takeaway: ebgp‑multihop is a tool for special topologies, not a default.

iBGP requires deliberate design choices because routers within the same Autonomous System must share routes learned externally without creating loops. Start with loopback peering: operators often configure iBGP sessions using loopback addresses as neighbor endpoints so the BGP session remains stable despite physical interface failures. However, using loopbacks changes the source IP of the TCP connection, so you must configure update‑source Loopback0 on the neighbor statement to force the router to use the loopback as the source. Equally important is reachability: the underlying IGP, such as OSPF or EIGRP, must correctly advertise those loopback addresses so the TCP connection can be established. The iBGP split‑horizon rule says a router will not advertise a route learned from one iBGP peer to another iBGP peer. That prevents loops but makes a naive iBGP deployment require a full mesh of peerings — every iBGP router peers with every other router — which scales as N*(N-1)/2. For larger networks, Route Reflectors or Confederations are used to reduce mesh requirements; we will cover those in a later chapter. A common troubleshooting mistake is forgetting to add update‑source, which leaves the neighbor stuck in Active because the source IP used by TCP does not match the configured neighbor IP. Takeaway: for stable iBGP, ensure loopback reachability, update‑source configuration, and an architectural plan for distribution.

BGP is built on top of TCP and uses port 179 as its standard transport. That means BGP relies on TCP’s reliable byte stream for ordered delivery and connection management; BGP messages are exchanged only after the TCP three‑way handshake completes. Practically, this implies that most session problems are TCP problems: if you cannot connect to port 179, the routers will not exchange OPEN messages and the neighbor state often remains in Connect or Active. A concrete troubleshooting step is to test TCP reachability with a telnet to port 179 from the router or an intermediary host. If telnet to 179 fails, inspect ACLs, firewall rules, or routing that prevents the source IP from reaching the peer. On iBGP with loopbacks, verify that the source address used for TCP is reachable and that update‑source was configured. Another common issue is incorrect remote‑as settings: if the remote AS does not match what the neighbor expects, the session may form TCP but fail during OPEN negotiation. Therefore, start by confirming TCP connectivity, then move to BGP message exchange and configuration. Misconception to avoid: assuming that BGP will retry infinitely without examining the underlying TCP connection or access controls — often the root cause is network reachability, not BGP syntax. Takeaway: when in doubt, validate TCP first, then BGP.

BGP defines five message types that drive session negotiation and route exchange. First is the OPEN message. Sent after the TCP handshake, OPEN negotiates version, the sender’s ASN, hold time, and router ID. If the parameters are invalid, the session will not establish. Second is UPDATE, the workhorse message that advertises and withdraws routes. An UPDATE contains prefixes plus a set of path attributes that describe characteristics and history for each route; path attributes allow policy decisions beyond simple reachability. Third is KEEPALIVE, a small periodic message sent to prevent Hold Time expiration and confirm the peer is alive. Fourth is NOTIFICATION: when a fatal error or protocol violation occurs, a NOTIFICATION is sent and the session terminates. Finally, ROUTE‑REFRESH requests a peer to re‑advertise routes, useful after applying a new policy without tearing down the session. Concrete example: after establishing TCP and exchanging OPEN messages, peers will exchange UPDATEs carrying prefixes; if you change policy and need new advertisements, you can request a ROUTE‑REFRESH rather than reset the whole session. Misconception: KEEPALIVE is not optional — without it the Hold Time will expire and the session will be declared down. Takeaway: each message has a distinct operational role and you will see them in debug output during session establishment and maintenance.

Now focus on the two messages you will most frequently reason about during session setup and routing: OPEN and UPDATE. OPEN is the negotiation handshake that follows TCP. It includes the sender’s ASN, the BGP version, Hold Time, and Router ID. If the Hold Time values differ, routers will agree on a value or refuse the connection depending on implementation; mismatched AS values cause the OPEN to be rejected. Once OPEN succeeds, UPDATE messages exchange routing information. An UPDATE advertises new reachable prefixes and can also withdraw previously announced routes. Critically, each UPDATE carries a set of BGP path attributes — pieces of metadata such as AS_PATH, NEXT_HOP, LOCAL_PREF, and others — that describe the route’s history and guide policy decisions. We will cover full attribute semantics in the next chapter, but for now remember that UPDATEs are far richer than a simple prefix list. Concrete example: when two peers come up, you might see an OPEN exchange then a stream of UPDATEs advertising the ISP's prefixes; when you apply a filter that removes certain routes, UPDATEs will send withdrawals for those prefixes. Misconception: UPDATEs do not only add routes; they also withdraw; watching both adds and withdraws is vital in debugging. Takeaway: OPEN sets the rules, UPDATE exchanges the data and policy-relevant attributes.

KEEPALIVE messages are the heartbeat of a BGP session. Sent periodically, they prevent the Hold Time timer from expiring. Without timely KEEPALIVEs or UPDATEs the peer will consider the neighbor down when the Hold Timer lapses. NOTIFICATION messages are sent when a router detects a fatal error; upon sending or receiving a NOTIFICATION the session is terminated so you can inspect the error code and reason. Practical debugging often encounters NOTIFICATIONs when an OPEN parameter mismatches or a malformed UPDATE is received. ROUTE‑REFRESH is a useful operational message: when you change route policies you can request a peer to re‑advertise its routes instead of tearing down the session. That helps avoid route flaps and preserves session state while policies take effect. A concrete operational example: after changing inbound filters you might use ROUTE‑REFRESH to ask the neighbor to resend its routes so your new filters are applied. A frequent misconception is that ROUTE‑REFRESH is mandatory on older implementations; modern BGP implementations support it as a standard mechanism to avoid session resets. Takeaway: KEEPALIVE maintains liveness, NOTIFICATION ends sessions with an error, and ROUTE‑REFRESH helps you reapply policy without resetting BGP.

The BGP neighbor state machine is the best place to start when sessions fail. It progresses through well‑defined states: Idle is the initial state where the process is not attempting a connection or is waiting to retry after an error. Connect means the process is waiting for the TCP connection to complete. Active indicates the process is actively trying to make a TCP connection; if TCP succeeds it moves to OpenSent. OpenSent means an OPEN was sent and the router awaits the peer's OPEN. OpenConfirm follows once an OPEN from the peer is received and the router waits for a KEEPALIVE or NOTIFICATION. Established is the final operational state where UPDATEs may be exchanged. Concrete troubleshooting workflow: if the neighbor is in Active or Connect, validate TCP to port 179, firewall rules, and routing to the neighbor. If it hangs in OpenSent or OpenConfirm, examine the OPEN parameters such as remote‑as and Router ID or use debug to watch OPEN and KEEPALIVE exchanges. A common misconception is to jump into BGP policy debugging while the neighbor never reached Established; policy is irrelevant until the session is up. Takeaway: map the observed state to the correct troubleshooting layer — TCP and reachability for Active/connect, OPEN validation for OpenSent/OpenConfirm, and UPDATE/policy for Established.

Let's walk through the hands‑on scenario provided in the chapter. You will configure two routers connected over a LAN and intentionally misconfigure the remote ASN on one side. On R1 you set router bgp 65001 and neighbor 192.168.12.2 remote‑as 65003. Because R2 is not configured or has a different ASN, the BGP neighbor will not reach Established; you’ll observe the neighbor in Active or OpenSent depending on whether TCP succeeds. The practical steps are: configure IP addresses on the connected interfaces, apply the first BGP configuration on R1 with the wrong remote‑as, and run show ip bgp summary to observe the neighbor state. Then configure R2 with router bgp 65002 and neighbor 192.168.12.1 remote‑as 65001; note the states shift but still may not reach Established until ASNs match. Finally correct R1’s neighbor configuration to remote‑as 65002 and watch the session transition to Established. Use debug ip bgp to observe OPEN, KEEPALIVE, and UPDATE messages during transitions. A common mistake is to forget to undo the incorrect neighbor before reconfiguring, which can leave stale entries; using no neighbor to remove entries is safe practice. Takeaway: the exercise reinforces the sequence: fix TCP and ASNs first, then inspect messages with debug.

When a BGP session fails, a systematic checklist saves time. Start with TCP: confirm connectivity to port 179 from the router or an intermediary host using telnet and show tcp brief. If TCP fails, inspect ACLs and firewalls before touching BGP. Next confirm ASNs: an incorrect neighbor remote‑as will block OPEN negotiation; ensure the remote‑as matches the intended peer. For iBGP, verify update‑source configuration and that the underlying IGP advertises the loopback addresses. A frequent real‑world error is forgetting to configure update‑source when peering to loopbacks — TCP may be sourced from a different IP than the configured neighbor, keeping the session in Active. Also verify that the correct interface addresses are used in neighbor statements and consider ebgp‑multihop only when necessary. Use show ip bgp neighbors to read the last error or NOTIFICATION code if the session dies. As a concrete checklist: 1) telnet to port 179, 2) verify route to neighbor IP, 3) check remote‑as values, 4) confirm update‑source for loopback peers, 5) review ACLs and firewall rules. Misconception: jumping to BGP policy changes before ensuring TCP and ASN correctness wastes time. Takeaway: work from transport up to BGP messages, and use the neighbor state to guide the checks.

Keep six core ideas top of mind as you work with BGP. First, eBGP is for peers in different Autonomous Systems and normally expects one‑hop adjacency. Second, iBGP is for peers within the same AS and requires planning because routers will not re‑advertise iBGP‑learned routes to other iBGP peers. Third, BGP uses TCP on port 179; when a session fails, verify TCP connectivity before deep BGP debugging. Fourth, the OPEN message negotiates session parameters and must match in meaningful ways for the session to form. Fifth, UPDATE messages carry prefixes and path attributes used for policy decisions, not just simple reachability. Sixth, KEEPALIVE preserves liveness and NOTIFICATION reports fatal errors. These concepts are foundational: use them as mental checks during configuration and troubleshooting. Ask yourself after each failure whether the problem is transport, negotiation, or routing policy, and that will guide your next steps.

Here are concise practical reminders you can carry into the lab. Always verify the remote ASN is correct — a single digit error prevents OPEN negotiation. For iBGP, ensure the IGP advertises loopback addresses and configure update‑source so the TCP source IP matches the neighbor configuration. When peering with an ISP, remember eBGP defaults assume one hop; only use ebgp‑multihop where topology requires it, and protect the peer with ACLs. Use show ip bgp summary and show ip bgp neighbors to map neighbor state to corrective action. Finally, use ROUTE‑REFRESH to reapply policies without resetting sessions and read NOTIFICATION codes when sessions terminate to target the root cause. These quick checks are highest value when you're under time pressure in operational environments. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.
